Everything a beginner needs to start calisthenics, built around a 5'9", 150 lb starting point, no equipment, and three focused hours a week. You are not underweight — you are under-muscled . Different problem, different fix. Daily calories ~2,800 kcal A lean bulk. Recalculate for your age and sex → Daily protein 150 g 1 gram per pound of bodyweight. The single most important nutrition number. Sessions 3 / week ~60 minutes each, full body, with a rest day between. Non-negotiable structure. Sleep target 7–9 hrs Muscle is built while you sleep, not while you train. Undersleeping halves your results. Year-1 potential +15–25 lb Realistic first-year muscle gain for an untrained male who eats and sleeps properly. The honest summary, in one paragraph. Pick a small number of hard movements. Do them 3 times a week. Every week, add a rep or make them slightly harder. Eat about 300 calories more than you burn, with 150 g of protein. Sleep 8 hours. Write down what you did. Do that for a year and you will not recognize yourself. Everything below is detail on top of those five sentences — the detail matters, but it is detail. You do not need to feel ready. Ready is built through repetition. What calisthenics actually is (and isn't) Calisthenics is strength training where the resistance is your own body. Push-ups, pull-ups, dips, squats, rows, core holds, and eventually skills like handstands and levers. It is not a separate species of exercise from lifting weights — it obeys exactly the same rules of physiology. Muscle grows when you give it a hard mechanical challenge, repeatedly, with enough recovery and enough protein. A barbell and a pull-up bar are two ways to deliver that challenge. What is genuinely different: What it does better Costs almost nothing. You can start today, on the floor, for $0. Builds control, not just force. Everything else — the program, the exercise ladders, the goals — is an application of what's here. If you understand this page, you can fix your own training forever instead of asking the internet. Muscle is expensive tissue. Your body will not build or keep it unless you give it a reason. The reason is mechanical tension : muscle fibers being forced to produce high force, repeatedly, close to their limit. Sensors in the muscle detect that tension, trigger a signaling cascade, and — if there is enough protein and enough rest — the fibers repair thicker than before. Two separate things improve, on two different clocks: Neural adaptation (weeks 1–8) Your nervous system gets better at using the muscle you already have: recruiting more motor units, firing them faster, and switching off the antagonist muscles that were fighting you. This is why your push-up count can double in a month with almost no visible change. Implication: early rep jumps are real strength but not yet size. Don't panic when the mirror lags the logbook by two months. Hypertrophy (weeks 6 onward) Actual growth of muscle fibers — more contractile protein laid down inside each cell. Slower, and completely dependent on eating enough and sleeping enough. A realistic ceiling for a well-fed untrained male is roughly 1–2 lb of muscle per month in year one, halving in year two, and halving again after that. Implication: your first year is the cheapest muscle you will ever buy. Don't waste it eating 1,800 calories. Connective tissue — tendons, ligaments, joint capsules — adapts on a third , much slower clock: months, not weeks. This mismatch is the single biggest injury risk in calisthenics. Your muscles will be ready for one-arm push-up attempts long before your elbows are. That's why the ladders on this site have rep gates before you move up: the gate isn't about your muscles, it's about buying time for your joints.

records.t: One sentence: if the demand does not increase, the adaptation does not continue. Your body adapts to exactly the stress you give it and then stops. Doing 3 sets of 10 push-ups every session for a year produces a person who is very good at 3 sets of 10 push-ups and otherwise unchanged. So every session needs a target that beats last time in at least one dimension. In a gym that's trivially "add 5 lb." With bodyweight you have to be more inventive — which is what the next section is about. The practical test. Open your log. Compare this week's session to the same session three weeks ago. If nothing is measurably harder — more reps, harder variation, slower tempo, less rest, more sets — you are maintaining, not building. Fix it this week.

records.h: 3 · The five levers: making a bodyweight exercise harder
records.t: You can't add plates to your body, but you have five independent dials. Turn one at a time . Turning three at once is how you jump from "too easy" to "can't do it" with nothing in between. Lever How it works Example Use when 1. Reps & sets More total work at the same difficulty. 3×8 push-ups → 3×12 push-ups → 4×12 Always your first move. Cheapest, safest, most measurable. 2. Leverage Change the angle or the distance between your hands and your center of mass, so the same bodyweight produces more torque. Incline push-up (hands on counter) → floor push-up → feet on a chair → pseudo-planche Reps have hit the top of your range (~15–20) and adding more is just cardio. 3. Range of motion Longer range = more work per rep, and more stretch under load, which is a strong growth stimulus. Push-up on the floor → push-up with hands on parallettes so your chest drops below your hands You want more stimulus without changing the movement you're practicing. 4. Tempo, pauses, and eccentrics More seconds of tension per rep; pauses kill the elastic bounce; slow lowering (eccentric) is where you are strongest and where most damage-and-repair happens. Normal push-up → 3 seconds down, 1 second pause at the bottom, 1 second up You have no way to change leverage right now (travel, no equipment) or you're building control for a skill. 5. Stability & limbs Take away a limb or a point of contact. Halving your base of support roughly doubles the demand on what's left, plus adds a big stability tax. Squat → split squat → Bulgarian split squat → shrimp squat → pistol squat The bilateral version is easy and you have no load to add. This is the answer for legs without equipment. There is a sixth lever once you own gear: added external load — a weighted backpack, a dip belt, a band. It's the most precise of all, which is why intermediate calisthenics athletes almost all end up using it for the basics while saving leverage work for skills. See Gear, Tier 2 . Rule of thumb for choosing a lever. If you can do more than ~20 clean reps, the exercise is no longer building much strength — change leverage (lever 2) or limbs (lever 5). If you can do fewer than ~5, it's too hard — go back a rung and use reps (lever 1) to build up. The productive band for a beginner is roughly 5–15 clean reps .

records.h: 4 · Sets, reps, and how much total work
records.t: What rep ranges do The old story — "1–5 for strength, 6–12 for size, 15+ for endurance" — is roughly directionally right but far too rigid. The current evidence says that if you take sets close to failure, anything from about 5 to about 30 reps builds a similar amount of muscle . What changes across the range is what else you get, and how unpleasant it is. Reps Primarily builds Notes for calisthenics 1–5 Maximal strength, neural efficiency Where skill work lives (one-arm push-up, muscle-up, lever holds). Hard on joints. Not where a beginner should spend most of their time. 6–12 Size, with good strength carryover Your home range. Best balance of stimulus, joint stress, and time. Most of this program lives here. 13–20 Size, muscular endurance Fine and useful, especially for legs, core, and early push-ups when you have no way to add difficulty. Sets get genuinely miserable near failure. 20+ Endurance; diminishing size returns Usually a signal you've outgrown the variation. Time to change a lever — not to do 50 push-ups. How many sets — the volume question Volume is normally counted in hard sets per muscle group per week (a "hard set" = a working set taken within a few reps of failure; warm-ups don't count). Below ~6 sets/week: maintenance at best. You will not grow much. 10–20 sets/week: the productive zone for nearly everyone. This program lands you around 10–14 per major muscle group, which is right for someone who is new and whose connective tissue is unconditioned. Above ~25 sets/week: returns flatten hard and recovery cost climbs. This is where beginners who read too many forums end up, get exhausted, and blame the program. Start at the low end. You want the smallest dose that still produces progress, because that leaves you room to add volume later when progress stalls. If you start at 25 sets a week, you have nowhere to go but sideways. Counting example. In this program, a push-up appears in Session A (4 sets), Session B (3 sets), and Session C (4 sets), plus dips and pike push-ups also hit the triceps and shoulders. So your chest is getting ~11 direct sets a week and your triceps closer to 16 including the indirect work. That is right in the productive zone. This is also why you don't need to add "arm day" — the arms are already working every session.

records.h: 5 · Proximity to failure — the RIR scale
records.t: RIR = Reps In Reserve : how many more clean reps you could have done when you stopped the set. RIR 2 means you stopped with two left in the tank. RIR 0 is true failure. RIR Feels like When to use it 4–5 Comfortable. Bar speed unchanged. Warm-up sets, deload weeks, technique practice, skill work. 2–3 Reps are slowing, you're working, but form is clean. Your default. Nearly all of your working sets, especially weeks 1–8. Almost all the growth, a fraction of the fatigue. 0–1 The last rep grinds; the next one would break down. Last set of an exercise, occasionally. Isolation and core work where failure is safe. Rep-max testing days. Beyond failure Form collapses, you cheat the rep out. Basically never as a beginner. It buys nothing extra and costs days of recovery. Beginners are systematically bad at judging RIR — studies find untrained lifters typically stop 4–6 reps earlier than they think they did. The fix is to occasionally take one set to true failure so you learn what the edge feels like. Once a week, on your last set of one exercise, go until you genuinely cannot complete a clean rep. Then calibrate everything else against that memory. Never take these to failure: anything overhead where a collapse drops you on your head (handstand push-ups, wall holds), anything where failure means falling from a bar with your body extended (front lever, muscle-up attempts), and skill work generally. Failure is for movements where the worst case is that you slowly sink to the floor.

Tempo is written as four numbers: eccentric / pause at bottom / concentric / pause at top . So a push-up at 3-1-1-0 means 3 seconds lowering, 1 second paused at the bottom, 1 second pressing up, no pause at the top. Eccentric (lowering) is the phase you're strongest in — you can lower about 1.3× what you can lift. That's the whole reason negatives work as a progression: you can train a pull-up before you can do one. Pauses at the bottom kill the elastic rebound and force the muscle to produce force from a dead stop in a stretched position. Brutally effective and completely free. The concentric should be intentional, not slow. Push with the intent to move fast even when the rep is grinding — that's what recruits high-threshold motor units. Default tempo for everything in this program: 2-0-1-0 . Two seconds down, no bounce, controlled up. If you find yourself bouncing, dropping, or using momentum, you are too high on the ladder — drop a rung.

Resting too little is the most common self-sabotage in bodyweight training, because sets feel "light" so people rush. Insufficient rest means your next set is limited by breathlessness rather than by muscular fatigue — which means less mechanical tension, which means less growth. Exercise type Rest Why Hard compound work (pull-ups, dips, push-ups, split squats) 2–3 min Full recovery of the phosphocreatine system; lets you actually load the muscle on set 3. Skill / max-strength practice (handstand, levers, negatives) 2–4 min Skill degrades with fatigue. Practicing tired teaches you the wrong movement. Core, calves, accessory 60–90 sec Smaller muscles, faster recovery, low systemic cost. Conditioning finisher 30–60 sec Here the breathlessness is the point. Superset your rest. A 60-minute session with 3-minute rests sounds impossible until you pair non-competing movements: do a push exercise, rest 90 s, do a pull exercise, rest 90 s, back to push. Each muscle still gets 3+ minutes, but you're never standing around. The program is built this way.

records.h: 8 · Frequency and why three full-body days wins
records.t: After a hard session, muscle protein synthesis stays elevated for roughly 24–48 hours in a trained person, then returns to baseline. If you only train chest once a week, that muscle spends five of seven days not growing. Hitting each muscle 2–3 times per week keeps it elevated more of the time — and the research consistently favors 2+ over 1 when weekly volume is matched. Three full-body days gives you: Every major pattern trained 3×/week — near-optimal frequency. Lots of practice reps of each movement, which matters enormously when the movements are also skills. Missing one day costs 33%, not 100%. With a 5-day bro split, missing leg day means legs get nothing that week. A full rest day between every session, which is exactly what unconditioned tendons need. The classic bodybuilding split (chest day, back day, arm day) works fine for people on their fourth year with 6 days to spend. For you, right now, it is strictly worse.

This is the single mechanism you'll use to advance for the next two years, so learn it properly. Every exercise gets a rep range and a set count . Start at the bottom of the range. Example: push-ups, 3 sets of 6, range 6–12. Each session, try to add reps to any set that isn't at the top of the range. 3×6 → 7/6/6 → 7/7/6 → 7/7/7 → 8/7/7 … When every set hits the top of the range (3×12) with clean form and 1–2 RIR, you have earned the next rung. Move to the harder variation and reset to the bottom of the range (e.g. 3×6 feet-elevated push-ups). It will feel like going backwards. It isn't — you are now producing far more force per rep. Repeat forever. Two properties make this work. First, it is self-regulating : bad sleep or a stressful week just means you add fewer reps, not that the program breaks. Second, it is unambiguous : you never have to guess whether you're ready to progress. The logbook tells you. When you stall. Failing to add a rep for two sessions in a row is noise. Three sessions is a stall. In that order, try: (1) sleep and eat more for a week; (2) add one set; (3) take a deload week ; (4) drop back one rung and rebuild. Do not just grind the same numbers for six weeks hoping it resolves.

Block Time What Why in this order General warm-up 5 min Raise body temperature: jog in place, jumping jacks, arm circles, leg swings. Break a light sweat. Warm muscle is more compliant and produces more force; cold tissue tears. Specific warm-up 5 min Wrist prep, scapular push-ups, scapular pulls, band pull-aparts, deep squat hold, then 1–2 easy sets of your first exercise. Primes the exact joints and patterns you're about to load. Wrists and shoulders especially. Skill practice 8 min Handstand or L-sit work, done fresh , well short of failure. Skills are nervous-system learning. Practice them tired and you learn the tired version. Main strength 30 min Your 2–3 hardest compounds — the pulling and pressing patterns — paired to overlap rest. Hardest work when you're freshest. This block is what drives the adaptation. Accessory & core 10 min Legs, core, and whatever's lagging. Shorter rests. Lower skill demand, so fatigue matters less here. Cooldown 3 min Easy stretching of what you just worked, nasal breathing, log your session. Mostly for the logging habit and to downshift. Stretching does not prevent soreness — but the logging genuinely matters.

Form advice online is 90% noise. Here is the whole thing in five rules: Full range of motion. Chest to the floor. Chin over the bar. Hip crease below the knee. Partial reps are the most common way people fake progress. If you can't do full range, the variation is too hard — regress. Control both directions. If you're falling rather than lowering, you're throwing away the most productive half of every rep. Brace your midsection. Before each rep: exhale slightly, then tighten your abs as if bracing for a punch, and squeeze your glutes. This locks your ribcage to your pelvis. Half of "bad push-up form" is just an unbraced core letting the hips sag. Breathe out on the effort. Inhale on the way down, exhale as you press or pull. Don't hold your breath through multiple reps. Move the joints through paths they like. Elbows around 45° from your torso in a push-up, not flared to 90°. Shoulders pulled down and back before you pull, not shrugged into your ears. Knees tracking over your toes, not collapsing inward. Everything else — hand width, foot position, exactly where you look — is personal and you will find your own version within a few weeks. The way to check your form without a coach: film one set from the side with your phone every couple of weeks. You will immediately see the sagging hips or the half-range reps that felt fine from the inside.

records.h: 12 · The six patterns that must all be trained
records.t: Programs go wrong when they become a list of favorite exercises instead of a balanced set of patterns. Every week you need all six. A good sanity check for any program: can you assign every exercise in it to one of these rows, and is every row occupied? Pattern Trains Your movements Horizontal push Chest, front delts, triceps Push-up family, dips (partly) Horizontal pull Mid-back, rear delts, biceps Inverted rows, table rows, band rows Vertical push Shoulders, triceps, upper chest Pike push-ups → handstand push-ups Vertical pull Lats, biceps, forearms, grip Pull-ups / chin-ups and their regressions Legs — squat & hinge Quads, glutes, hamstrings, calves Squat → split squat → pistol; glute bridge → Nordic curl Core — anti-extension & anti-rotation Abs, obliques, deep stabilizers, hip flexors Dead bug, hollow hold, plank family, leg raises, L-sit Balance push and pull roughly 1:1, and if anything, favor pull. Almost everyone starts with a strong-ish chest and a weak upper back, then does more push work because it's easier and more visible. The result is rounded shoulders, a forward head, and eventually shoulder pain. Extra rows are the cheapest insurance in all of training.

records.h: 13 · Twelve mistakes that will cost you months
records.t: Mistake What it costs Fix Program hopping every 3 weeks Everything. No program can show results before ~8 weeks. Commit to 12 weeks before you judge anything. Not logging workouts You cannot apply progressive overload if you don't know last week's numbers. Use the tracker. Every set, every session. Half-range reps to inflate the count Trains a shorter, weaker range and lies to your logbook. Full range or regress. Film yourself monthly. Eating like you're trying to stay 150 lb The most common reason a skinny beginner sees no change. You literally cannot build tissue from a deficit for long. Eat ~2,800 kcal, 150 g protein. Too much push, not enough pull Shoulder pain in month 4–8, and a physique that looks worse from behind. Match or exceed push volume with pull volume. Skipping legs The classic calisthenics look: big arms on chicken legs. Also worse athleticism and a weaker core. Legs every session. They're in the program for a reason. Chasing advanced skills in month 1 Muscle-up and front lever attempts on unconditioned tendons cause elbow and shoulder tendinopathy that lasts months. Earn the rep gates. They exist to protect connective tissue. Rushing rests to "keep the burn" Turns strength training into cardio. Less tension, less growth. Time your rests. 2–3 min on compounds. Training through sharp or joint-line pain Turns a 2-week annoyance into a 6-month problem. Read the pain rules . Sharp, joint-located, or worsening = stop. Sleeping 5–6 hours Directly and measurably reduces muscle gain, increases fat gain, and blunts strength. 7–9 hours, consistent bedtime. Protocol. Adding 40 minutes of "extra" work because you feel good Recovery debt that shows up two weeks later as a stall. Do the program. Add volume deliberately, not emotionally. Comparing yourself to Instagram Demoralization, then quitting. Those are 5–15 year training ages, often with unusual leverages and sometimes drugs. Compare to your own logbook from 8 weeks ago. That's the only honest comparison.

Term Meaning Rep One complete execution of a movement, start to finish. Set A group of reps done back to back without rest. Hard / working set A set taken within ~3 reps of failure. The kind that counts toward volume. RIR Reps In Reserve — how many you left in the tank. RPE Rate of Perceived Exertion, 1–10. RPE 8 ≈ RIR 2. Two scales for the same thing. Concentric The shortening/lifting phase — pressing up out of a push-up. Eccentric / negative The lengthening/lowering phase. You're ~30% stronger here, which is why negatives are a progression tool. Isometric A hold with no movement — plank, L-sit, handstand, dead hang. Progression / regression A harder / easier version of the same movement pattern. Volume Total work, usually counted as hard sets per muscle per week. Deload A planned easy week to let fatigue dissipate and connective tissue catch up. Scapular retraction / depression Pulling your shoulder blades together / pulling them down away from your ears. The setup position for nearly every pull. Hollow body Ribs down, lower back pressed flat, pelvis tucked. The fundamental calisthenics core position. Straight-arm strength Force produced with elbows locked (planche, lever, L-sit). Loads tendons far more than bent-arm work — earn it slowly. GPP General physical preparedness — baseline conditioning that lets you recover between sets and sessions. DOMS Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness. Peaks 24–48 h after training. Not a measure of a good workout. TDEE Total Daily Energy Expenditure — the calories you burn per day, all in. Exercise library Every movement, arranged as a ladder Calisthenics has no dumbbell rack, so difficulty comes from ordered progressions instead. Each ladder below runs from "you can do this today, at 150 lb, with no equipment" to genuinely advanced. Each rung has a gate : the exact performance that earns you the next rung. How to use this page. Every rung carries its own setup, execution, the one cue that matters, and the mistake people actually make on it — open Setup & execution under any rung. You do not do every exercise here. You pick one rung per ladder — whichever one puts you in the 5–15 clean rep range — and that is your exercise until you clear its gate. The rung finder picks that rung for every ladder in about two minutes, and the program tells you which ladders to use on which day. Come back here when you clear a gate, or when something hurts and you need a regression. Five minutes, every session, before anything else. Wrists and shoulders take the most abuse in calisthenics and get the least attention; this is what keeps them healthy. Wrist prep sequence 2 min · every session Your wrists are about to hold your entire bodyweight in extension — a position they never otherwise experience. Do all of these on the floor, 10 slow reps or a 20-second hold each: Palms down, fingers forward. Rock forward and back over your hands, keeping palms glued down. Palms down, fingers pointing back at your knees. Rock gently backward. This one stretches the forearm flexors hard — go easy. Backs of hands down, fingers pointing back. Rock gently. Stretches the extensors. Fists down, knuckles flat. Rock forward and back. Builds the option to train on fists when wrists are cranky. Fingertip pushes. On all fours, push down through fingertips only, 10 reps. Wrist circles , 10 each direction, with fingers interlaced. Why it matters: wrist pain is the #1 reason beginners abandon handstand work. Two minutes a session prevents almost all of it. Shoulder prep: dislocates, pull-aparts, scapular work 2 min · every session Towel/band dislocates × 10. Hold a towel wide overhead, arms straight, and take it back behind you and return. Go wider if it pinches. Never force it. Band pull-aparts × 15. Arms straight in front holding a light band, pull it apart to chest level, squeezing shoulder blades together. Best single exercise for beginner shoulder health. Scapular push-ups × 10. In a push-up plank with locked elbows , let your chest sink between your shoulder blades, then push the floor away and round your upper back. Only the shoulder blades move. Scapular pulls × 10 (once you have a bar). Hang with straight arms, then pull your shoulder blades down and back to raise your body an inch or two. No elbow bend. This is the missing skill in 90% of failed pull-ups. Arm circles 10 forward, 10 back, big and slow. Lower body prep: leg swings, deep squat hold, ankle rocks 1–2 min Leg swings 10 front-to-back and 10 side-to-side per leg, holding a wall. Deep squat hold, 30–60 s. Sit in the bottom of a squat, heels down, elbows inside knees pushing them out. If your heels lift, put a book under them and work toward flat. Ankle rocks × 10/side. Half-kneeling, drive your knee forward past your toes keeping the heel down. Ankle mobility is the hidden limiter in pistol squats. Glute bridges × 15 to wake up the glutes before squatting.

records.t: Trains: pectorals, front deltoids, triceps, serratus anterior, and (if you brace properly) the entire anterior core. This is your bread and butter for the first year. Wall push-up Gate: 3 × 20 Cue Squeeze your glutes so your hips do not lead or trail — the whole body moves as one plank. Setup & execution Equipment Nothing but a wall. Stand an arm's length from a wall, hands flat on it at chest height and slightly wider than your shoulders. Step your feet back until your body is a straight line from ears to heels. Bend your elbows to bring your chest to the wall over two seconds, then press back. Most common error Standing too close, which turns it into an arm bend with no load. First time This will feel too easy, and that is correct. You are teaching your shoulder blades and your midsection to hold one rigid line. Nothing should hurt. If your wrists complain, put your hands on fists instead. Too hard? If your hips sag or your shoulders shrug up to your ears, step in closer to the wall and take a set off. Too easy? 3 sets of 20 clean reps with a two-second lower. Then move to a kitchen counter. High incline push-up (counter) Gate: 3 × 15 Cue The higher your hands, the easier it is — use that to dial the difficulty precisely. Setup & execution Equipment A kitchen counter, a windowsill, or a solid desk at roughly hip-to-chest height. Don’t have it? A wall at first, then the back of a heavy couch pushed against a wall. Any fixed surface works — what matters is that it cannot slide. Hands on a kitchen counter or a solid desk, slightly wider than your shoulders, feet walked back so your body is a straight diagonal. Lower until your chest touches the edge, elbows tracking about 45° from your torso, then press away. Most common error A surface that slides or tips. Push on it hard before you trust it. First time Your triceps will tell you about it the next day more than your chest will. That is normal at this angle. Push hard on the surface before you trust it with your weight. Too hard? If your chest cannot touch the edge without your hips dropping, use a higher surface. There is no penalty for going higher. Too easy? 3 sets of 15 with your chest touching the edge every rep. Then drop to a chair seat. Low incline push-up (chair) Gate: 3 × 15 Cue Push the floor away rather than thinking about lifting yourself — it keeps the shoulder blades from collapsing. Setup & execution Equipment A chair seat, a stair, or the arm of a couch — roughly 18 inches up. Don’t have it? The second or third step of a staircase gives you every height between here and the floor. It is the most adjustable free equipment you own. Hands on a chair seat, a stair, or the arm of a couch, roughly 18 inches up. Same straight line and same 45° elbows; chest touches the surface each rep. Most common error Letting the hips sag as the angle gets harder. If they sag, go back to a higher surface. First time This is the rung where most people first feel their chest working rather than just their arms. Make sure the chair is against a wall so it cannot slide out from under you. Too hard? If the last two reps break form, move up one stair. Half a step is a real jump in difficulty at this height. Too easy? 3 sets of 15 with your chest touching the surface. Then either drop a stair or switch to knee push-ups. Knee push-up Gate: 3 × 15 Cue Hips fully extended. If you are folded at the hip this becomes a much shorter, much easier rep. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. A folded towel or a rug under the knees if the floor is hard. Kneel with your knees a foot or so behind your hips, hands under your shoulders, and cross your ankles. Push your hips forward until you are a straight line from knees to head, then lower your chest to the floor and press up. Most common error Sitting back toward your heels, which shortens the lever and skips most of the work. First time Watch for the hip fold — it is the near-universal fault here and it makes the rep about a third shorter. Film one set

records.t: Trains: lower chest, triceps (heavily), front deltoids. Dips are the closest bodyweight equivalent to a heavy press and are worth building toward. They are also the movement most likely to irritate a shoulder, so respect the depth rule below. Bench dip, knees bent Gate: 3 × 15 Cue Keep your back close to the chair — drifting forward puts the shoulder in a bad position. Setup & execution Equipment A chair, bench, step, or bed edge. Don’t have it? The edge of a bathtub, a low wall, or a stair. Anything solid at roughly knee height. Sit on the edge of a chair, hands beside your hips gripping the edge, fingers forward. Slide your hips off the front, knees bent and feet flat and close. Lower until your upper arms are parallel to the floor, then press back up. Most common error Dropping below parallel because it feels easy. Depth is where dips hurt people. First time Bench dips put your shoulders in an internally rotated position that some people simply do not tolerate. If the front of your shoulder pinches, stop and use push-ups and pike push-ups for your triceps instead — this whole ladder is skippable until you have parallel bars. Too hard? Bring your feet closer in and take more weight through your legs. Reduce the depth if your shoulders complain. Too easy? 3 sets of 15. Then straighten your legs. Bench dip, legs straight Gate: 3 × 15 Cue Shoulders stay pressed down away from your ears at the bottom. Setup & execution Equipment A chair, bench, or step. Don’t have it? Same as above. Same, with your legs extended and only your heels on the floor. Longer lever, more of your weight on the arms. Most common error Shrugging at the bottom, which is the position that irritates shoulders. First time Keep your back close to the bench. Drifting forward is what turns shoulder discomfort into shoulder pain here. Too hard? Bend your knees again and walk your feet in. Too easy? 3 sets of 15 with legs straight and a controlled depth. Then elevate your feet. Bench dip, feet elevated Gate: 3 × 12 Cue Treat this as a stepping stone, not a home. Get to parallel bars. Setup & execution Equipment Two chairs, or a chair and a step. Don’t have it? A bench and a coffee table. Heels on a second chair so your body is level between the two. Lower to parallel and press. Most common error Living on this rung. The behind-the-back arm position gets less shoulder-friendly the harder it gets. First time This is the top of what a chair can give you. Do not chase depth here — go find parallel bars or rings instead, which are both safer and better. Too hard? Lower the feet, or go back to legs straight on the floor. Too easy? 3 sets of 12. Then move to parallel bars if you have access to them. Parallel-bar support hold Gate: 3 × 30 s Cue Actively push down through the bars. A passive hang in the support position is what you are training out of. Setup & execution Equipment Parallel bars, dip bars, gymnastic rings, or two very solid chair backs. Don’t have it? A park has parallel bars. Two kitchen counters facing each other work if they are the right distance apart. Jump or step up between parallel bars with your arms locked straight. Push your shoulders down away from your ears, brace your core, point your toes, and hold completely still. Most common error Swinging your legs. Stillness is the skill here. First time Shoulders down and away from your ears, elbows locked. This hold is what conditions the shoulder and elbow before you start loading them through range — do not skip it to get to real dips faster. Too hard? Keep a toe on the ground to take weight off. Hold for less time rather than breaking the shape. Too easy? 3 sets of 30 seconds with locked elbows and depressed shoulders. Then negatives. Negative dip (5s down) Gate: 3 × 5 Cue Slight forward lean held constant through the descent. Setup & execution Equipment Parallel bars or rings, and a step to get to the top. Don’t have it? Jump or step up to the top position from the floor. Get to the top support posi

records.t: Trains: deltoids (all three heads), triceps, upper traps, and the whole overhead stability system. This is how you build shoulders without a barbell, and it doubles as handstand preparation. Incline pike push-up Gate: 3 × 12 Cue Hips high. The higher the hips, the more this is a shoulder press and not an incline push-up. Setup & execution Equipment A chair or a low table. Don’t have it? A bed edge or a couch arm works. Stairs let you fine-tune the height. Hands on a chair, walk your feet in and push your hips up high so your torso is as close to vertical as your hamstrings allow. Lower the top of your head toward the seat between your hands, then press back up. Most common error Straight legs at the cost of a rounded back — bend the knees instead. First time Hips high is the whole game. The higher your hips, the more this is a shoulder press and the less it is an incline push-up. Too hard? If your back rounds trying to get your hips high, bend your knees. Rounded back with straight legs is worse than a bent-knee pike every time. Too easy? 3 sets of 12 with your head touching down between your hands. Then take it to the floor. Floor pike push-up Gate: 3 × 12 Cue Your head goes down between your hands; your chest does not travel forward. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. From a push-up position walk your feet toward your hands into a downward-dog shape. Hands slightly wider than shoulders. Lower the crown of your head to the floor between and slightly in front of your hands, so head and hands form a triangle. Touch lightly, press straight back up. Most common error Letting the hips drop, which turns it into a decline push-up and takes the shoulders out of it. First time Your head goes down between your hands and your chest does not travel forward — head and hands make a triangle. Expect far fewer reps than a normal push-up; your shoulders are much smaller than your chest. Too hard? If your hips drop and your chest travels forward, it has become a decline push-up. Go back to the chair. Too easy? 3 sets of 12 with a light head touch. Then elevate your feet. Feet-elevated pike push-up Gate: 3 × 10 Cue This is a genuine overhead press — treat the reps with the same respect. Setup & execution Equipment A chair or couch. Don’t have it? A bed, or the second stair. Feet on a chair or couch, hands on the floor, hips stacked high so your torso is close to vertical. Same head-to-triangle path, same lockout. Most common error Raising the feet so high that you cannot control the descent to the floor. First time This is a genuine overhead press now. Treat the reps with the respect you would give a barbell over your face. Too hard? If you cannot control the descent, lower the feet. You should never be dropping the last few inches onto your head. Too easy? 3 sets of 10 under control. Then move to wall walks and start the handstand line. Wall plank / wall walk Gate: 60 s hold Cue Push tall through your shoulders the whole time, as if trying to make yourself an inch taller. Setup & execution Equipment A clear wall and about four feet of floor. Move anything breakable. Start in a push-up position with your feet against the base of a wall. Walk your feet up the wall and your hands in toward it, a few inches at a time, until your body is vertical and your chest is close to the wall. Hold, then walk back out under control. Most common error Walking your hands in further than you can walk back out from. First time Being upside down is disorienting the first few times and your heart rate spikes. That fades within two or three sessions. Learn to walk back out before you go all the way in. Too hard? Walk your hands out a few inches. Only ever walk in as far as you can walk back out from. Too easy? A 60-second hold close to the wall. Then chest-to-wall handstand holds. records.t: Trains: latissimus dorsi, biceps, brachialis, forearms and grip, lower traps, rhomboids, and core. If you only did one calisthenics exercise for life, this would be it. It is also the pattern you cannot properly train without a bar — which is why a $30 doorway bar is the highest-ROI purchase on this site. Dead hang Gate: 60 s accumulated, one unbroken 30 s Cue Grip hard and breathe normally. This builds the grip that otherwise caps your pull-ups. Setup & execution Equipment A pull-up bar. This is the Tier 1 purchase that unlocks the phase. Don’t have it? A playground bar, a scaffolding pole, a tree branch thicker than your wrist, or the top of a door frame if your fingertips can take it. Grip the bar just outside shoulder width with your thumbs wrapped around it. Hang with straight arms and let your shoulders relax up toward your ears, then pull them down away from your ears and hold. Alternate relaxed and active hanging. Most common error Dropping off the bar. Step or lower down — dropping is how wrists and shoulders get tweaked. First time Your hands will give out long before your arms do, and the skin on your palms will complain for the first two weeks before it toughens. Wrap your thumbs around the bar. Never drop off — step or lower down. Too hard? Keep your toes on the ground and take some weight off. Accumulate the time in short sets. Too easy? 60 seconds of accumulated hang, including one unbroken 30 seconds. Then scapular pull-ups. Scapular pull-up Gate: 3 × 10 with a visible 2-inch rise Cue Elbows stay locked. If they bend, it has become a tiny pull-up and you have skipped the skill. Setup & execution Equipment A pull-up bar. Don’t have it? Same substitutes as the dead hang. Hang with completely straight arms. Without bending your elbows at all, pull your shoulder blades down and back so your whole body rises an inch or two. Hold for a second, lower under control. Most common error Rushing. This is the position every pull-up starts from, and most failed pull-ups skip it. First time An inch or two of movement is the whole rep, and it looks like nothing. This is the position every pull-up starts from, and most failed pull-ups fail because this was skipped. Too hard? If your elbows bend it has become a tiny pull-up. Keep your toes down and practise the movement with less weight. Too easy? 3 sets of 10 with a visible two-inch rise and locked elbows. Then add band assistance. Band- or foot-assisted pull-up Gate: 3 × 8 on your lightest band Cue Take only as much help as you need — the band should make the last two reps possible, not the whole set easy. Setup & execution Equipment A pull-up bar and a resistance band, or a bar low enough to keep your toes down. Don’t have it? A low bar, a sturdy table edge, or a partner holding your feet. Two chairs and a broomstick work if the broomstick is sound. Loop a resistance band over the bar and put one knee or foot in it, or use a bar low enough to keep your toes on the ground. Set your shoulder blades down and back, then pull your elbows toward your ribs until your chin clears the bar. Lower over three seconds. Most common error Living on a heavy band forever. Step down a band as soon as you can get eight reps. First time Bands snap back. Set your foot in the loop deliberately and keep your face out of the line of the band if it slips. Too hard? Use a thicker band. Take only as much help as you need — the band should make the last two reps possible, not the whole set easy. Too easy? 3 sets of 8 on your lightest band. Then negatives. Negative pull-up (5s down) Gate: 3 × 5, last rep still 5 seconds Cue Fight the whole way down, especially the last third where most people just drop. Setup & execution Equipment A pull-up bar and something to step up on. Don’t have it? A chair beside the bar, or jump to the top position. Jump or step up so your chin is over the bar. Hold there for a second, then lower yourself for a slow five-count until your arms are completely straight. Step back up

records.t: Trains: rhomboids, mid and lower traps, rear deltoids, lats, biceps. This is the anti-hunchback pattern and the most-skipped exercise in beginner calisthenics — partly because it's the hardest to improvise. Do not skip it. Doorway towel row Gate: 3 × 15 with feet well forward Cue Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end of each pull and hold for a second. Setup & execution Equipment A door and a towel. Nothing else. Don’t have it? A sturdy table edge, a fence rail, or a post. Anything you can grip and lean back from. Loop a towel around a solid door handle with the door open, and stand on the hinge side so it cannot swing shut. Hold both ends, walk your feet forward and lean back with straight arms, then pull your chest toward your hands. Most common error Only bending your elbows. Without the shoulder-blade squeeze this is a biceps curl. First time Loop the towel around the handle with the door open and stand on the hinge side, so the door cannot swing shut on you. This is the free substitute that keeps your back training honest before the bar goes up. Too hard? Walk your feet back so you are more upright. The more upright you stand, the easier it is. Too easy? 3 sets of 15 with your feet well forward. Then get under a table. Table row, knees bent Gate: 3 × 12 Cue Body straight from knees to head — do not let the hips sag toward the floor. Setup & execution Equipment A solid dining table. Don’t have it? A desk, a low bar, or two chairs with a broomstick across them — test it hard first. Lie under a sturdy dining table, grip the edge with both hands about shoulder-width, knees bent and feet flat. Brace your core, then pull your chest to the underside of the table and lower under control. Most common error Trusting a table you have not tested. Push up on it hard first and weight the far side if it can tip. First time Check the table can hold your weight and cannot tip — weigh the far side down if you need to. This is the single most valuable free exercise you have; your back has no other good bodyweight option before the bar. Too hard? Walk your feet in toward you and stay more upright. Bent knees with feet close is the easiest version. Too easy? 3 sets of 12 with your chest touching the underside. Then straighten your legs. Inverted row, legs straight Gate: 3 × 12 Cue Lead with the elbows and finish by pinching the shoulder blades together. Setup & execution Equipment A table, a low bar, or rings at hip height. Don’t have it? A table works for all of this. Rings or a bar are kinder on the wrists. Same setup but with your legs straight and only your heels on the floor. Chest touches the bar or table edge every rep. Most common error A head-first reach. The chest travels, not the chin. First time Your hips will want to sag. One line from heels to head, and your chest touches — not your stomach. Too hard? Bend your knees again, or raise the bar. Higher bar equals easier row. Too easy? 3 sets of 12 with your chest touching and your body in one line. Then elevate your feet. Feet-elevated inverted row Gate: 3 × 12 Cue Keep the glutes squeezed — the higher the feet, the more the hips want to sag. Setup & execution Equipment A low bar or table, plus a chair for your feet. Don’t have it? Any box, step, or stack of books at roughly bar height. Heels on a chair so your body is horizontal or slightly head-down. Everything else is the same, with more of your weight on your arms. Most common error Raising the feet before you can do twelve clean flat-footed reps. First time With your feet level with the bar this is close to a horizontal bodyweight row, which is a genuinely hard pull. Rep counts drop. Too hard? Lower the feet. Every few inches counts. Too easy? 3 sets of 12 with feet level with the bar. Then archer rows. Archer row Gate: 3 × 8 /side Cue Hips stay square. Rotating to reach the bar defeats the purpose. Setup & execution Equipment A low bar or rings. Don’t have it? A table edge, though the hand position is more awkward.

records.t: Trains: quadriceps, glutes, adductors, and — once you go single-leg — a huge amount of balance and hip stability. Bodyweight squats stop being a strength exercise for a healthy 150 lb person within a few weeks. The answer is single-leg work, which is why the ladder moves there fast. Box squat Gate: 3 × 15 Cue Touch, do not flop. Controlling the last inch is the whole point. Setup & execution Equipment A chair, bench, or bed edge. Don’t have it? A stack of books, a low stool, or a step. Higher is easier. Stand in front of a chair, feet shoulder-width and toes turned slightly out. Push your hips back and sit down until you just touch the seat, then stand up by driving through your whole foot. Most common error Letting the knees fall inward as you stand. Push them out over your second toe. First time Push your hips back first, not down. Touch the seat, do not sit and rest on it. If your heels lift, put a folded towel under them and work on your ankles separately. Too hard? Raise the surface. Sitting to a higher box is a legitimate month of training, not a failure. Too easy? 3 sets of 15 touching the seat under control. Then squat without the chair. Bodyweight squat Gate: 3 × 20 Cue Heels stay down. If they lift, put a book under them and work on ankle mobility. Setup & execution Equipment Nothing. Feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out, arms forward for balance. Sit down between your hips until the crease of your hip is below your kneecap, keeping your heels flat and chest up, then stand. Most common error Stopping at parallel because it is easier. Below parallel or it is a partial. First time Knees tracking over your toes is fine and normal. Knees collapsing inward is not — push them out as you stand. Most people find depth is limited by their ankles, not their knees. Too hard? Put the chair back. There is no shame in a target. Too easy? 3 sets of 20 with your thighs at least parallel to the floor. Then move to one leg at a time. Split squat Gate: 3 × 12 /leg Cue Straight down, not forward. Your torso stays over your hips. Setup & execution Equipment Nothing. A wall or chair back for balance if you need it. Step one foot forward into a stance about two to three feet long, both feet flat and pointing forward. Lower straight down until your back knee is an inch off the floor, then press through the front foot to stand. All reps on one leg, then switch. Most common error A stance too short, which jams the front knee and cramps the back leg. First time Single-leg work exposes a strength difference between your sides that you probably did not know about. Do your weaker leg first and match the stronger one to it. Too hard? Hold a wall with one hand, or shorten the range so your back knee stops higher. Too easy? 3 sets of 12 per leg with your back knee lightly touching down. Then elevate the back foot. Bulgarian split squat Gate: 3 × 12 /leg Cue Most of your weight on the front foot — the back leg is a kickstand, not a driver. Setup & execution Equipment A chair, bench, or step for your back foot. Don’t have it? A couch, a bed, or a low windowsill. Around knee height. Stand two to three feet in front of a chair and place the top of your rear foot on it. Lower straight down until your rear knee nearly touches and your front thigh is at or below parallel, then drive through the whole front foot. Most common error Falling over and giving up. Hold a doorframe with one hand for the first few sessions. First time This is the hardest leg exercise most people ever do without a barbell, and it is brutal the first time. Expect three or four days of soreness. Start with two sets, not three. Too hard? Lower the back foot, or go back to split squats. Too easy? 3 sets of 12 per leg. Then start pistol work. Assisted / box pistol squat Gate: 3 × 8 /leg to a low box Cue Reach both arms forward as a counterweight — it is the difference between standing up and falling backward. Setup & execution Equipment A low box, chair, or stair, and something to hold

records.t: Trains: glutes, hamstrings, spinal erectors. Squatting patterns barely touch the hamstrings, and calisthenics athletes are famous for having none. This is the fix, and it also protects your knees and lower back. Glute bridge Gate: 3 × 20 Cue Squeeze the glutes to lift, do not arch the lower back to lift. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. A mat or carpet is kinder on your spine. Lie on your back with knees bent and heels close to your butt, arms flat at your sides. Drive through your heels to lift your hips until your body is a straight line from knees to shoulders, squeeze the glutes hard for two seconds, then lower. Most common error Pushing off your toes. Drive through the heels. First time You should feel this in your glutes. If you feel it mostly in your lower back or hamstrings, you are arching rather than squeezing — tuck your pelvis before you lift. Too hard? Reduce the range — lift to where you can still feel your glutes rather than your lower back. Too easy? 3 sets of 20 with a two-second squeeze at the top. Then move to one leg. Single-leg glute bridge Gate: 3 × 15 /leg Cue Hips stay square — if one side drops, lower the range and build up. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. Same setup with one foot planted and the other knee pulled toward your chest. Drive up through the planted heel, keeping your hips level side to side. Most common error Rushing. Two seconds up, two-second squeeze, two seconds down. First time Your hips will want to drop on the unsupported side. Keep them level — that is most of the exercise. Too hard? Go back to two legs, or keep the non-working foot lightly touching down. Too easy? 3 sets of 15 per leg with level hips. Then elevate your shoulders. Shoulder-elevated hip thrust Gate: 3 × 15 Cue Finish with a hard glute squeeze at the top and ribs down. Setup & execution Equipment A couch, bed, or bench to rest your shoulder blades on. Don’t have it? A sturdy chair pushed against a wall, or a step. Sit on the floor with your upper back against the edge of a couch, knees bent, feet flat and about shoulder-width. Drive your hips up until your torso is parallel to the floor, chin tucked, then lower. Most common error Hyperextending the lower back at the top instead of finishing with the glutes. First time The extra range is the point. Make sure whatever you rest on is against a wall — this is a movement that slides furniture. Too hard? Go back to floor bridges, or reduce the range. Too easy? 3 sets of 15 with a full lockout and a two-second squeeze. Then sliding leg curls. Sliding leg curl Gate: 3 × 10 Cue Hips stay high the entire time. The moment they drop, the hamstrings stop working. Setup & execution Equipment Two towels on a hard floor, or furniture sliders. Don’t have it? Paper plates on carpet, or socks on hardwood. Both work. Lie on your back with your heels on towels or furniture sliders on a hard floor. Bridge your hips up, then slowly slide your feet away until your legs are almost straight, and curl them back in — all without letting your hips touch down. Most common error Extending further than you can curl back from. First time Only works on hardwood, tile, or laminate. Your hamstrings will cramp the first couple of times — that is normal for a muscle that has never been trained through this range. Too hard? Use both legs, shorten the range, or push through your hands on the way back out. Too easy? 3 sets of 10 keeping your hips up throughout. Then single-leg Romanian deadlifts. Single-leg Romanian deadlift Gate: 3 × 12 /leg, slow Cue Hips square to the floor — do not let the free-leg hip rotate open. Setup & execution Equipment Nothing. A wall for fingertip balance. Don’t have it? A backpack with books adds load once bodyweight is easy. Stand on one leg with a soft knee. Hinge at the hip, letting the free leg extend straight behind you as your torso lowers, until you feel a strong stretch in the standing hamstring. records.t: Small, easily trained, and completely ignorable until you notice your calves haven't changed in a year. They respond to high reps and a full stretch. Standing calf raise — 3 × 25, full range, 2-second pause at the top. Single-leg calf raise on a stair — heel drops below the step for a deep stretch, rise to full tiptoe. 3 × 15–20 per leg. This is the version that actually works at 150 lb. Seated / bent-knee calf raise — targets the soleus underneath. Put a loaded backpack on your knee while seated. 3 × 20. Tibialis raises — back against a wall, feet out in front, pull your toes up toward your shins. 3 × 20. Prevents shin splints and balances the ankle.

Trains: rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, obliques, hip flexors. The core's real job in calisthenics is resisting movement — keeping your body a rigid lever. That's why holds beat crunches here. Dead bug Gate: 3 × 10 /side, no lower-back gap Cue Press the lower back down so hard nobody could slide a hand under it. If it lifts, shorten the reach. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. Lie on your back with arms pointing at the ceiling and knees bent at 90° over your hips. Press your lower back flat into the floor. Slowly lower one arm overhead and the opposite leg toward the floor, then return and switch sides. Most common error Going fast. Three seconds out, three seconds back. First time Press your lower back flat into the floor and keep it there. If it lifts, you have reached too far — that is the entire skill, and it transfers to every other movement on this site. Too hard? Reach less far, or keep your knees bent. Range is the dial here. Too easy? 3 sets of 10 per side with no gap under your lower back. Then hold a plank. Plank Gate: 3 × 60 s Cue Actively brace as if bracing for a punch — a plank you can hold for three minutes is not a plank, it is a rest. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. A mat helps your elbows. Forearms on the floor under your shoulders, feet together, body in one line. Squeeze the glutes, tuck the pelvis slightly, pull the ribs down, and push the floor away so the upper back is not collapsed. Most common error Adding time past sixty seconds. Add difficulty instead. First time A plank is not about how long — it is about how hard. Squeeze your glutes, tuck your pelvis, and pull your elbows toward your toes. Done properly, 60 seconds is plenty. Too hard? Drop to your knees, or put your forearms on a chair. Shorten the hold before you break the line. Too easy? 3 sets of 60 seconds in a straight line with the pelvis tucked. Then tuck hollow holds. Tuck hollow hold Gate: 3 × 45 s Cue Lower back glued to the floor. That contact is the entire exercise. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. Lie on your back and press your lower back flat. Lift your shoulders and head slightly off the floor, arms reaching forward, and hold your knees tucked toward your chest. Most common error Straining the neck. Keep a tennis-ball-sized gap under your chin. First time Lower back pressed flat is the requirement. The moment a gap appears, the set is over — no matter how long you have held it. Too hard? Tuck tighter, or put your hands on your thighs. Too easy? 3 sets of 45 seconds with your lower back glued to the floor. Then extend one leg. One-leg hollow hold Gate: 3 × 45 s Cue Extend only as far as you can keep the back flat. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. From the tuck hollow, extend one leg out straight and low while keeping the other tucked. Alternate legs between sets. Most common error Extending both legs before one is easy. First time Swap sides between sets. The lower the extended leg, the harder it gets — that is your fine adjustment. Too hard? Bend the extended leg, or raise it higher. Higher is easier. Too easy? 3 sets of 45 seconds per side with a flat lower back. Then extend both legs. Full hollow hold Gate: 3 × 45 s Cue The lower the arms and legs, the harder it gets — use that as the dial. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. Arms extended overhead by your ears, legs straight and low, shoulders and heels both off the floor, lower back pressed flat. The most transferable core position in calisthenics. Most common error Letting the back arch to get the legs lower. Raise the legs instead. First time This is the shape underneath the handstand, the front lever, and a good push-up. Time spent here pays out across the whole site. Too hard? Raise your legs and arms higher, or tuck one knee. Too easy? 3 sets of 45 seconds. Then start rocking. Hollow rock Gate: 3 × 20 Cue The body stays one rigid banana-shaped piece; only the contact point moves. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. A mat or carpet — this is uncomfortable on

records.t: Lying knee tuck Gate: 3 × 20 Cue Keep the lower back pressed down throughout. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. Lie on your back with your hands tucked under your hips for support. Pull your knees toward your chest, lifting your hips slightly off the floor at the top, then lower under control without letting your feet touch down. Most common error Swinging the legs to build momentum. First time Lower back stays flat. Hands under your tailbone is a legitimate assist, not cheating. Too hard? Put your hands under your tailbone, or reduce the range. Too easy? 3 sets of 20 with your lower back flat. Then straighten your legs. Lying straight-leg raise Gate: 3 × 15 Cue Stop lowering at the point where the back would arch — that point is your current range. Setup & execution Equipment Floor. Same position with legs straight. Raise them to vertical, then lower until just before your lower back lifts off the floor, and raise again. Most common error Letting the back arch to get the legs lower. That is where lower-back pain comes from. First time The moment your lower back arches off the floor, the set is over. That point is usually much higher than people expect. Too hard? Bend your knees slightly, or stop the legs higher off the floor. Too easy? 3 sets of 15 with your heels reaching the floor and your back still flat. Then take it to the bar. Hanging knee raise Gate: 3 × 15 Cue Pause for a full second at the bottom of every rep to kill the swing. Setup & execution Equipment A pull-up bar. Don’t have it? A playground bar, or dip bars in a support hold. Hang from the bar with shoulders active. Raise your knees above hip height, curling the pelvis slightly at the top, then lower slowly to a full hang. Most common error Using a body swing to throw the knees up. First time Your grip will fail before your abs do for the first month. That is normal and it is why dead hangs are in the program. Control the swing — if you are pendulum-ing, you are using momentum. Too hard? Tuck tighter and raise less high. Or go back to the floor version until your grip catches up. Too easy? 3 sets of 15 with no swing. Then straighten your legs. Hanging straight-leg raise Gate: 3 × 12 Cue Point your toes and keep the legs locked — bent knees are the easier version. Setup & execution Equipment A pull-up bar. Don’t have it? Same as above. Hang with active shoulders and legs straight, toes pointed. Keeping the knees locked, raise your legs to horizontal or above, curling the pelvis slightly at the top, then lower over three seconds to a full hang and pause before the next rep. Most common error Kipping. If you cannot do it strictly, go back to knee raises. First time Hamstring flexibility limits this as much as strength does. If you cannot reach horizontal with straight legs, that is usually your hamstrings talking. Too hard? Bend the knees. Any amount of bend takes load off. Too easy? 3 sets of 12 with straight legs to horizontal. Then toes to bar. Toes to bar Gate: 3 × 8 Cue Lean back slightly and pull with the lats to get the last part of the range. Setup & execution Equipment A pull-up bar with room above and in front. Don’t have it? Same as above. From a hang, raise your legs all the way until your feet touch the bar between your hands, then lower with control. Most common error Turning it into a kipping swing to reach the bar. First time Strict toes to bar is genuinely hard. The version you see done fast with a kip is a different exercise; do not compare yourself to it. Too hard? Stop at horizontal. Toes to bar is a long way past horizontal. Too easy? 3 sets of 8, toes touching the bar, without swinging. The L-sit ladder Foot-supported L-sit Gate: 3 × 20 s Cue Push your shoulders down away from your ears. That is the strength you are actually building. records.h: Filming your own form — the self-check lists
records.t: You cannot see your own form, and the way something feels from the inside is a poor guide to what it looks like. Sagging hips feel level. Half-range pull-ups feel full. This is the closest thing to having a coach that costs nothing: film one working set from the side every two to four weeks , then run it against the checklist for that lift. How to film so the video is actually useful Side view, at hip height. Prop the phone on a stack of books about 6–8 feet away. Front-on hides almost every error worth finding; the side view shows spine position, range, and joint angles. Whole body in frame, including hands and feet, for the entire set. Film a real working set, not a demo rep. Errors appear under fatigue — reps 6–10 are the informative ones. Use slow motion if you're checking tempo or a specific sticking point. Keep the clips. A push-up from week 1 next to week 12 is more convincing than any measurement. Watch it twice: once for range of motion, once for everything else. Trying to see everything at once means you see nothing. Universal checks — run these on any lift Did every rep reach the same end position? Compare rep 1 to the last rep. Range shrinking under fatigue is the most common and most self-deceiving error. Is the lowering controlled or falling? Count the seconds. If the eccentric is under one second, you're throwing away half of every rep. Is the spine holding one shape throughout? Any point where the lower back suddenly arches or the upper back rounds is where the core gave out. Are the two sides doing the same thing? One shoulder rising, one hip shifting, one knee caving. Asymmetry under load is worth addressing early. Is there a pause and a lurch? A hitch at one point in the range is a weak position — that's where pauses and partials should be applied. Push-up Look for What it means Fix Hips lower than the line of shoulders-to-heels Core isn't bracing; lower back is taking the load Squeeze glutes and tuck the pelvis. If you can't hold it for the whole set, regress a rung. Hips higher than the line (piking) Usually an unconscious way to shorten the range Straight line ears to ankles; watch the video, not the feel. Chest stops 3+ inches off the floor Partial reps Regress a rung until full range is possible. Elbows out near 90° from the torso Shoulder-impingement position Tuck to about 45°. Arrow shape from above, not a T. Head reaching for the floor ahead of the chest Neck compensating for missing range Neutral neck; eyes on a spot a foot in front of your hands. Hips rising first on the way up Chest is the weak link; you're leading with the legs Push the floor away as one rigid piece. Add pauses at the bottom. Pull-up and chin-up Look for What it means Fix Arms not fully straight at the bottom Cutting the hardest part of the range Full dead hang every rep. Fewer full reps beats more partials. Shoulders up by the ears at the start No scapular set — the pull has nothing to start from Depress and retract the shoulder blades first. Drill scapular pull-ups. Legs swinging or kicking Kipping; the reps aren't strict Cross your feet, squeeze glutes, hold a slight hollow. Chin barely clears, chest far from the bar Range ending early Aim the collarbones at the bar, not the chin over it. Dropping fast from the top Discarding the eccentric 2–3 seconds down, every rep. Elbows drifting forward at the top Biceps doing the work the lats should Drive elbows down and back toward your ribs. Inverted row Look for What it means Fix Hips sagging toward the floor Core disengaged; the row becomes an arm exercise Glutes and abs tight, one straight line heels to head. Chest not touching the bar or table edge Partial range Walk your feet in to make it easier and finish every rep. Shoulders rolling forward at the bottom No scapular retraction — back is doing nothing Pinch the shoulder blades together and pause one second at the top. Head jutting toward the bar Neck compensating for missing range Neutral neck; the chest travels, not the chin.

records.h: The six rules that make this work
records.t: Pick your rung from the ladders , not from ego. The correct rung is the one where the bottom of the rep range is genuinely hard and the top is currently out of reach. If you can already do the top of the range, move up. If you can't hit the bottom with clean form, move down. Use double progression . Add reps until every set hits the top of the range, then move up a rung and reset to the bottom. That's the whole progression mechanism, forever. Stop 2–3 reps short of failure on everything except the final set of each exercise, where 1 RIR is fine. Weeks 1–2, stop 4 short. You are building tendons, not testing yourself. Rest as long as the table says. If you are short on time, superset two neighbouring movements that do not compete — do set 1 of the first, rest, set 1 of the second, rest, and go back. Each muscle still gets its full rest while you are never idle. Click any rest figure to see why it is what it is. Log every set, every session. Exercise, rung, reps per set, and how it felt. The tracker does this. Without a log there is no progressive overload, only guessing. Never skip the warm-up, and never skip legs. These are the two things beginners cut when short on time, and they are the two that cost the most.

What you need: nothing you have to buy. The floor, a wall, a sturdy chair, and either a dining table you can get under or a door with a towel over the handle. That is the entire equipment list for four weeks. The Tier 0 list spells it out, and every movement below tells you what to use instead if you are missing something. Goal: build the habit, learn the six patterns, condition your connective tissue, and establish a logbook. Three sets of three main movements is the whole session — you should finish every one in weeks 1–2 feeling like you could have done more. That is the design, not a compromise. Volume ramps automatically: week 1 is about 60% of the sets listed, week 2 about 80%, weeks 3–4 the full amount. Today's session does that arithmetic for you. records.h: How to actually run a session
records.t: Before you start: open your log from last time. Write down the exact numbers you're trying to beat today. Do not train without a target — "see how it goes" is how weeks disappear. Warm up properly. 5 minutes general, 3 minutes specific. Then do one easy set of your first exercise at about half the reps. Skill work while fresh. Short sets, long rests, never near failure. If your handstand holds are getting worse rather than better within the block, the block is over — move on. Main lifts in pairs. A1, rest 90 s, A2, rest 90 s, A1… Set a timer; don't eyeball it. Write each set down as you finish it. Not at the end from memory. Note anything unusual: bad sleep, a tweaky elbow, a rep that felt great. Finish with core and accessories at shorter rests, then two minutes of easy stretching for whatever you just worked. Eat within a couple of hours with 30–40 g of protein. The old 30-minute "anabolic window" is a myth, but total daily protein absolutely is not.

A deload is a planned easy week. Fatigue from training accumulates faster than you notice; a deload lets it dissipate so the next block starts fresh, and it gives tendons and joints — which adapt far more slowly than muscle — a chance to catch up. How to deload: keep the same exercises and the same rungs, but cut sets roughly in half and stop 4–5 reps short of failure on everything. Keep skill practice (it's low fatigue and high value). Do not take the week completely off — total rest loses more than it gains, and it breaks the habit. Signal Meaning Reps declining for 2+ sessions across multiple exercises Accumulated fatigue. Deload now, don't wait for week 6. Joints ache before you even start warming up Connective tissue hasn't caught up. Deload and reassess your rungs. Resting heart rate up 5+ bpm for several days Systemic fatigue or you're getting sick. Dreading sessions you used to look forward to Real and predictive. Deload. Sleep getting worse despite being tired Classic overreaching sign.

You are trying to gain weight, so you don't want to burn enormous amounts of energy. But some cardio is genuinely valuable: it improves recovery between sets and sessions, it's strongly protective for long-term health, and at these doses it will not interfere with muscle gain. Type Dose When Why Zone 2 (easy) — brisk walk, easy bike, easy jog where you can hold a conversation 2–3 × 25–40 min/week Rest days or after training Builds the aerobic base that determines how fast you recover between sets. Very low interference with strength. Daily walking 7,000–10,000 steps Throughout the day Health, appetite regulation, and it keeps a lean bulk lean. Costs nothing in recovery. Intervals / sprints Optional, 1 × 10–15 min/week max Not the day before or after leg-heavy sessions Good conditioning, but expensive in recovery and it competes directly with leg training. Optional for a beginner. Long runs (5+ miles) Not while bulking — High interference with strength and a big calorie sink. Revisit later if you want to run.

Situation What to do Missed one session Nothing. Do it the next day, or skip it and continue. Do not double up. Missed a whole week Resume at the same rungs but cut one set for the first week back. You lose almost nothing in a week. Missed 2–4 weeks Repeat the last week you completed at 2–3 sets and 4 RIR, then resume. Expect soreness. Strength returns much faster than it was built. Only have 20 minutes Do the minimum effective session : 3 sets of your push rung, 3 sets of your pull rung, 3 sets of your squat rung, all supersetted with 60 s rest. That is 80% of the benefit in a third of the time. Sick — symptoms above the neck (runny nose, sore throat) Train at reduced intensity if you feel up to it. Cut sets in half. Sick — symptoms below the neck (fever, chest, body aches, GI) Do not train. Rest until you're a full day symptom-free, then resume at deload volume. Still very sore from last session Train anyway but reduce sets — light movement usually reduces soreness. If it's severe enough to change your form, swap in a different pattern for that day. Traveling with no space or gear Push-ups, split squats, hollow holds, table rows, and a doorway towel row cover every pattern in a hotel room. Keep the habit even at reduced quality. Terrible sleep last night Train, but drop to 3 RIR and skip the last set of each exercise. Don't try to set records on 5 hours of sleep.

By week 24 you should be doing sets of strict pull-ups and dips, holding a wall handstand, and squatting on one leg. At that point you are no longer a beginner and the linear "add a rep every week" approach starts to sputter. Three sensible directions: Weighted basics. Keep the same three-day structure and just add weight to pull-ups, dips, and push-ups. Boring, and by far the most reliable way to keep getting bigger and stronger. Skill specialization. Pick one goal — freestanding handstand, muscle-up, front lever — and give it a dedicated block with the basics on maintenance volume (about half your current sets). Add a fourth day. An upper/lower or push/pull/legs/skill split, if 3 days is no longer enough stimulus and your recovery is genuinely good. What you should not do is switch to a completely different program because progress slowed. Slowing down after six months is not a sign the program failed. It's a sign it worked, and you're now a more advanced trainee for whom progress is simply slower. That is permanent, and it happens to everyone. Previous ← Exercise library Next Goals & metrics →

records.h: The baseline test — do this on day one
records.t: Twenty minutes, once, before you train. These numbers are irreplaceable: in six months you will badly want to know where you started, and there is no way to go back and get them. Repeat the identical test at weeks 9, 12, and 24, and then every 12 weeks forever. Protocol Warm up for 5 minutes — light cardio plus wrist and shoulder prep. Don't test cold. Rest 3 full minutes between every test. This is a strength test, not a circuit. One attempt per test. Every rep must be full range with clean form — a half rep is not a rep . Stop the set the moment form breaks, not when you physically cannot move. Test in this exact order every time. Order affects results, so it has to be constant. If you can't do a movement at all, write 0 . Zero is a real, useful data point — it's the one that will look most dramatic later. # Test Standard Record 1 Max push-ups Chest to the floor, body straight, no rest at the top. Stop when you break form. Reps 2 Max pull-ups (overhand) Dead hang start, chin fully over the bar, no kipping. No bar? Write "n/a" and test max inverted rows instead. Reps 3 Max inverted / table rows Body straight, chest touches the bar or table edge. Note your foot position so you can replicate it. Reps + setup 4 Max dips (bench or bars) Upper arms to parallel. Note which version. Reps 5 Max pike push-ups Head touches the floor between your hands. Reps 6 Max bodyweight squats Hip crease below the knee, heels down. Cap at 50 — beyond that it's a cardio test. Reps 7 Max split squats, left and right Rear knee to an inch off the floor. Record each leg separately — asymmetry is worth knowing about. Reps L / R 8 Plank hold Forearms, hips level, stop when they sag. Cap at 3 minutes. Seconds 9 Hollow hold Your best rung with the lower back flat. Note which rung. Seconds + rung 10 Dead hang From a bar, until your grip gives out. Seconds 11 Wall handstand hold (chest to wall) If you can get up at all. Otherwise record your best wall-walk position. Seconds 12 Deep squat sit Heels flat, how long can you sit at the bottom of a squat comfortably? A mobility, not strength, marker. Seconds Log it in the tracker. The tracker page has a baseline-test form that stores all twelve numbers with a date, so retests sit next to the original and you can see the deltas at a glance. Do the rung finder right after this. The baseline test tells you where you are; the rung finder turns that into which version of each movement to actually train. Two minutes, and it saves into today's session .

records.h: What to measure, and how often
records.t: Metric Frequency How Why it matters Every set you do Every session Exercise, rung, reps per set, RIR The only way progressive overload happens. Non-negotiable. Bodyweight Daily, ideally Wake up, use the bathroom, weigh nude, before eating or drinking. Track the 7-day average , never a single day. Daily weight swings 2–4 lb from water, salt, and food volume. Only the weekly average is signal. Tape measurements Every 4 weeks Same time of day, same conditions, relaxed not flexed. See below . Catches muscle gain that the scale hides and shows you where it's landing. Progress photos Every 4 weeks Same spot, same light, same clothing, same poses. See below . The single most convincing evidence, because you can't see gradual change in a daily mirror. Baseline retest Weeks 9, 12, 24, then quarterly The exact protocol above. Objective proof of strength gain that isn't confounded by which rung you happen to be on. Sleep hours Daily Rough estimate is fine — bed time and wake time. When progress stalls, this is usually the culprit, and you'll only spot it if you tracked it. Calories & protein Daily for the first 4 weeks, then spot-check A food app; weigh food for the first two weeks to learn portions. Almost everyone is wrong about how much they eat until they measure it once. Resting heart rate Daily if you have a watch On waking, before getting up. A sustained 5+ bpm rise is an early fatigue or illness warning. Do not measure daily what changes monthly. Weighing daily is fine because you average it. Taking photos or tape measurements weekly is actively harmful — the change is smaller than the measurement noise, so all you see is randomness, and it reads as failure. Four-week intervals, minimum.

Keep them in the tracker. The tracker stores your photos on this device — no upload, no account, nobody else can see them — and puts any two of the same pose side by side with the number of days and the bodyweight change between them. That side-by-side is the single most convincing thing you will see all year. You look at yourself every day, so you are the person least able to notice your own change. Photos four weeks apart are shockingly effective, but only if the conditions are constant. Otherwise you're comparing lighting, not muscle. Same time of day — first thing in the morning, fasted, after the bathroom. Food and water visibly change your midsection. Same place, same light. Overhead room lighting, not a window — daylight changes with the season and time. Same clothing — shorts or underwear, no shirt. Same clothes every time. Same phone position — mark a spot on the floor with tape, prop the phone at the same height, use a 10-second timer. Four shots: front relaxed, side relaxed, back relaxed, and front flexed. The relaxed ones are the honest ones; the flexed one is the fun one. Stand normally. Don't suck in on day one and pose hard on day ninety, or you'll fool yourself in both directions. Never delete the early ones, even if you hate them. Especially if you hate them.

Use a flexible cloth or plastic tape. Snug enough not to sag, loose enough not to compress the skin. Measure relaxed for the record (you can also record a flexed arm for fun, but keep the two separate). Take each measurement twice and average.
